speechtext:
We have a standing rule, number 15, which lays down very strictly the program for the complete week. It defines what shall be taken up on Monday, on Tuesday, and so on, and that procedure is very strictly adhered to. There would be a nice fuss if there was any proposal to deviate from it without unanimous consent. But in connection with this matter, the right of private members to bring in resolutions, it does not need general consent at all. The program as laid down provides that Monday shall be devoted to the introduction of private members' resolutions. Wednesday is only a half day and private members have Thursday for the first four weeks. But that is only a trick of language, because as a matter of fact it is not four weeks, but only three weeks. The first Thursday cannot be counted because private members cannot discuss any resolutions on that day. Why not be honest and call it three weeks? That was thought reasonable at one time and perhaps it was then, but the gradual increase in the number of groups suggests that greater opportunity should be afforded for private members to debate matters in which they are interested. After a time the government moves that one of the days allotted to private members each week be discontinued, and a little later another day is taken away. This means blocking discussion.
Before last session I placed a notice on the order paper at least six weeks prior to the meeting of the house. Under ordinary conditions, in any company or public board, notice of that length of time would be sufficient to get a motion heard; but although I placed my motion on the order paper six weeks before the house met it had only reached the top of the list, about to come on for discussion, when the Prime Minister rose and moved that all further private members' days be taken away. This year I thought I would make sure and I therefore placed a resolution on the order paper three weeks after the close of the house. That surely was plenty of time. On July 25 I sent the notice in. Now I am second on the list and my resolution may or may not be heard. I do not think it will be. And twenty-five members with resolutions below mine cannot possibly be heard. Thursdays we have already lost because we debated the speech from the throne and the Bren gun for three weeks. But we discussed the speech from the throne on the motion of the Prime

Minister that it should take precedence, though he was well aware that in that way we were going to be deprived of three or four Mondays and Wednesdays. In the British Columbia legislature it is the custom-it is very frequently done, at any rate-to have a member or two speak on the address and then adjourn that debate and go on to some other public business on the order paper. But that was not done here; it never is, and in that way private members' days are taken away and they have no opportunity to discuss resolutions in which they are interested. The Prime Minister is now taking away one of the private members' days before we have had, even for one day, the opportunity to which we are entitled. This is the first time it has ever happened. We have not had a private members' day so far this session, and now, as the scripture says, the government is taking away the semblance of the privilege-"that which he seemeth to have." That is not democracy.
We have heard before, and I am sure the Prime Minister will tell us again, that there are a number of other opportunities available to us. One of these is the occasion when estimates are in committee of the whole. We are told that we can then deal with any subject in which we are interested. But that is limited by the fact that in committee there is a strict rule which provides that speeches in committee of the whole must be relevant to the item or clause under discussion. I have been caught in that way before. It may easily be that there will be no item in the estimates under which some particular subject which hon. members would like to discuss might properly be taken up, so that that outlet is closed. The other alternative is the time-honoured one, "Oh well, you can always discuss it on the motion to go into supply," that being the occasion on which under the old British tradition, members 'are allowed to voice grievances before granting supply. The answer is this. It is a well-known fact, indeed, it is one of the rules, that an amendment to the motion to go into supply constitutes a vote of want of confidence in the government. Can anyone expect therefore that members elected to support the government will take such a step when it might mean the defeat of the government? Still less can you expect the government to extend sympathetic consideration, let alone taking sympathetic action, on a resolution framed in such a way that, if carried, it would mean their own defeat.
That is why I say that we should not be deprived of these opportunities to introduce resolutions for discussion. Very often a resolution is brought in and defeated and on another

Precedence lor Government Business
occasion it is brought up again. The government hear what is going on and the people of the country become educated in the idea that is advocated and express their views privately to the government. Subsequently it may be brought forward in a more acceptable form and one or other of the parties adopts it as their policy. It is therefore educative and useful.
It may be said that a good part of the session has already gone and we have done nothing. But the address in reply to the speech from the throne is a part of the government's business. Apart from custom, there is no law that makes it incumbent upon the government, when they have little or no business of their own, to adjourn the house. They might go on to private resolutions. But they never do; instead they adjourn the house. There have been two Friday evenings that we could have made use of in the discussion of private members' resolutions, but on both occasions the house was adjourned.

speechtext:
The motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) must be considered in conjunction with the larger question of reorganizing the rules of procedure of the house. Private members' privileges are being taken away every year. I have a motion on the order paper and I have no objection to letting it go this year in order to get on with the business, because all these motions might be considered under the estimates; but we have a parliamentary constitution and we have rules, and yet private members have few or no privileges. Some ten years ago and almost every year since I introduced a motion which would have remedied the present situation, and in the last four years I have discussed the subject matter of that motion, namely, the revision of the rules of the house, together with constitutional reform, parliamentary reform, cabinet reform and law reform. It took three hundred years for parliamentary government to attain its present control over the budget and the executive, and in the struggle there was bloodshed. When
parties cannot agree there is always trouble. The constitutional changes that have been brought about in the motherland have not come about without a great deal of sacrifice, and where two sides could not agree there was trouble, as in the case of the general strike in 1926 when troops were sent to the docks.
My proposal is that we should set up a committee to study the question of our rules and procedure, and of parliamentary, constitutional, cabinet and law reform, and reform in other directions. We have no control over the constitution or the exchequer at the present time. We are simply conducting post mortem examinations. For example, this afternoon we have been hearing something about an international trade treaty that was passed over the heads of parliament, and of industry and labour. I do not refer in any spirit of criticism to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, or done because I believe he did at heart what he believes to be right. But, I repeat, we should have a committee on law reform and on House of Commons reform to bring our proceedings up to date. On the order paper there are many bills having to do with the criminal code, bills embodying amendments which private members think should be made. Some of these are proposed by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and some by other hon. members, and in my opinion there should be a standing committee on legal bills and estimates to which these questions could be referred. There are a number of standing committees to-day. I have been a member of one committee that has not met in years, the public accounts committee. We should revise our ways of doing business and adopt the municipalities' plan of dealing with estimates. The heads of departments sit around a table with a committee and strike off thousands here and there, or perhaps half a million. subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext: That is not correct. At any time the government, with its huge majority, could have adjourned any debate and gone on with any business.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext: We could not have adjourned the debate on the address in reply, because a motion was carried by this house that it should have precedence over everything else. And I ask hon. members what would have been said of the government if we had, as suggested, adjourned the Bren gun debate.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext: You did adjourn it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext: However, I am not anxious to get into any controversy or argument; I am simply stating the plain facts. I ask myself, what do the people of this country expect the government to do? Do they expect the government to be governed by private members, or by its own appreciation of the necessity of doing the business of this country?

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext: To be governed by parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
We have been sent here for the purpose of carrying on the business of this country. The business of the country is not primarily private members' motions, it is the business which the government brings forward.
I come to what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) said, because I agree that this whole situation has a much larger significance than appears in this resolution. He said to-day that many assemblies in the world have been swept out of existence because the people thought they had become incapable of carrying on the business of government. That was his statement. There are a great many people in this country who are busily at work trying to develop a similar agitation against democratic government. I could direct his attention without much difficulty to agitation in some quarters to have it appear that this country is without leaders, that parliament is incapable of carrying on business and that we should have something different. It would be very easy to have the people content to slip into the fascist method of doing business should the country be given the impression that the government, because of the time taken up by private members, has no opportunity to go ahead with the business of the country.

Precedence for Government Business
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) says they have been denied four private members' days this session. We have been denied, by the discussions that have taken place in this house, nine government days.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15

speechtext: After voting twice against the motion, my hon. friends turned around and supported the motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
Each house manages its own affairs. It is part of my obligation, and I do it in no critical way, but from a sense of duty, to point out some of the circumstances governing this situation, which are responsible for the rules of the house being what they are. The rules of the house are to protect all hon. members, and by following them carefully and literally we shall get along much further with both private and public business. What I wish to make perfectly plain at this moment is that the government have been sent here by the people of Canada to carry on the business of the country, and the first duty of parliament is to get on with that business, no matter what anyone may say or wish. When private members, whether through resolutions or any other circumstances whatever, occupy the entire time of parliament so that it is impossible for the government to get on with a single measure, then I say the time has come for the government to take such action as is necessary and imperative to see that it can get ahead with the public business.
I have no desire to be arbitrary in this matter. If it will assist in restoring a sense of cooperation at the present time I have no objection to changing the date in this resolution from the fifteenth to the twenty-second. I think, however, that is as far as we should go at the present time. Monday still remains for a consideration of private members' resolutions. speechtext: Another thing I wish to point out. There are two houses of this parliament, the Senate and the House of Commons. The cost of carrying on the work of parliament relates to both houses. Now thus far this session the senate, through no fault of the government, has had no legislation at all from this house. We have been unable to send any legislation across to the other house. They are adjourning again, waiting for legislation from this side. Private members' resolutions do not go to the other house.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext: But in no ease has Wednesday been taken away before we ever had a single day's discussion.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
I have not gone through Hansard to see, as my hon. friend will probably understand. But may I point out that when the government does get on with its own business there is opportunity at those times, as has been pointed out. for private members to discuss many of the matters contained in their own resolutions, matters which are of great nublic
Precedence

for Government Business
concern. There is nothing which restricts private members from debating every question of government business.
My hon. friend speaks of the number of resolutions and says many of them will not be reached. When we find difficulty in discovering a proper procedure under our own rules we very often go, in fact it is one of the rules that we should go to the parliament at Westminster and see what procedure is followed there. What is done at Westminster with regard to private members' resolutions? Do they try to run through all that appear on the order paper and debate every resolution? They do not. They have a ballot; a limited number of resolutions are selected by ballot, and those are the only ones permitted to be taken up. If the rules and practices at Westminster were studied you would see wherein the present administration has been, if anything, more than lax in not insisting before this on the right of the government to get under way with its own business. It is not with any desire to curtail the opportunities of private members that I am asking the house to accept this resolution with the date amended to the twenty-second; it is simply because I know only too well that before this parliament ends every hon. member will be anxious enough to get through with government business as rapidly as possible.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
I certainly must correct the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in some of his statements. Let me say to him at once that I do not object very seriously to the practice of taking away Wednesday some time after the session has moved along and an opportunity has been given for the discussion of private members' measures, and later in the session taking away Monday, as is usual. But in the present instance I do not think the right hon. gentleman has been quite reasonable in his attitude.
In regard to last Friday, the government had on the order paper a bill regarding pensions, one with respect to fisheries, a resolution concerning the granting of $100,000 to the city of Ottawa, a resolution regarding the penitentiaries commission, a resolution concerning technical education, and I think also the resolution regarding the national film board. These were all before us on the order paper; they were reached; any one of them might have been called. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) had his bill under consideration for some considerable time and then the discussion was adjourned because of questions that were put to him from his own side as well as 
from this side of the house. The minister, I think quite properly, let certain clauses stand, but there was no obstruction or difficulty; substantial progress was made. Then the resolution of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) with regard to authority to appropriate $750,000,000 was discussed and adjourned by the government. We could have gone on with that if the government had wished so to do. All these measures were there to be gone on with, last Friday.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
The government was not
ready.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
Not only that; in other
years I have seen it happen in the early part of the session, when the government business was not ready, that we would go right through the order paper to private members' resolutions. The Prime Minister repeatedly said that the government had been prevented from getting on with its own business. Control of the house is always in the hands of the government, and from my recollection that was never more so than it is to-day, having regard to the government's huge majority. The Prime Minister asks what we would have thought if they had suggested adjourning the debate on the address after passing the resolution at the commencement of the session that it should take precedence over all other business. That is the regular resolution, but it was not necessary. Four or five years ago we debated the speech from the throne over a period of weeks but as an ordinary item on the order paper, without a resolution establishing precedence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
Did my hon.
friend approve of that?

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON AND AFTER WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 15
speechtext:
I did not; generally
speaking I prefer the present method. But there was nothing at any time to hinder adjournment of the debate by the government for the purpose of taking up any other matter. Certainly there was nothing to hinder adjournment of the Bren gun discussion at any time and the taking up of other orders of business. I want to make it abundantly clear that on Friday night the government were not prepared to go on with their business and that so far as we were concerned, there were five or six items which could have been proceeded with. We were quite willing to go on. In fairness to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) I must add that I believe there was a sort of understanding on Friday between the whips that the house should adjourn at six o'clock.
Now that the Prime Minister takes the attitude he does I think we should make it perfectly clear that had any such wish been

Royal Visit
expressed by the government we would have been quite willing to proceed with the business. My hon. leader was not here but I know that my colleagues and myself would have gladly agreed to go on. I am not reproaching the government for what it did, but I do say the Prime Minister is not treating the house fairly in seeking to lay the onus for all this on the shoulders of those who sit on this side of the house, because there was an abundance of government measures to proceed with had they so desired.
As to the suggestion that we are to have supply backed up until the end of the session, once again that is in the hands of the government. During the coming months they may do as they wish in connection with supply; and to say, after the house has been sitting for four or five weeks, that there is any question about the discussion of supply is drawing a pretty wild bow.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that it is not reasonable to ask this. He has consented to let the motion stand for a week. I think it would be quite proper to question it even then, because under the rules there is plenty of opportunity for government business to be proceeded with.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty) of which I gave notice yesterday. My question is with reference to the visit of their majesties,
and with reference to certain publications which appear on news stands and reading rooms throughout the country. I refer directly to Scribner's magazine of February 11. particularly to page 16, a copy of which I gave to the Postmaster General yesterday. In that publication there is a statement that our king is a usurper, that he was a weak personality and only on probation, and that he is not the legal occupant of the throne. The article makes use of many other epithets which I know every Canadian would resent. Further, the text of the article was sent to Canada in a dispatch of a United States newspaper group, and was published in many Canadian daily papers.
Under the rules of the House of Commons no member may speak disrespectfully of his majesty or of any member of the royal family; yet periodicals, which have been commented on in England, are circulating here. Scribner's went farther in this article and published a lot of pictures from the Chicago Tribune-a mere invention.

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister ot hinance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.
Mr. T. C. DOUGLAS (Weyburn) Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I desire to bring up a matter which is of vital importance not only to the people I represent but also to thousands of others who live in the drought areas of western Canada. I have no wish whatsoever to hold up supply, and I shall take only a few minutes to present to the house what I believe to be a matter of urgent public importance. I refer to the need for relief seed in those areas of western Canada where, because of drought, rust and grasshoppers, the farmers will not have sufficient seed to sow their crops this spring.
I am aware of the fact that the distribution of seed comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. But I am also aware of the fact that during the past two years this parliament has passed a seed grain bill placing a federal guarantee behind loans for the purchase of seed in western Canada. Parliament has thus indicated its interest and its responsibility in the matter.
On January 27 of this year, as reported at page 380 of Hansard, the hon. member for Qu Appelle (Mr. Perley) asked a question of the government with respect to its intention
in this matter for the present year. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) replied that no request had come to him for assistance in connection with the financing of seed grain purchases. I do not think the provincial governments, and especially the government of Saskatchewan, will be able to finance relief seed this spring, without federal assistance. I cannot but think that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has already discussed this matter with the western provincial governments. He must have some policy in mind regarding this important subject. It is because I should like to have him enunciate that policy at this time that I bring the matter to the attention of the house.
There are only three matters I should like to place before the government, the first of which concerns the urgent need for governmental assistance in connection with procuring seed for the farmers in the drought area this coming spring. It is a well known fact that the provincial governments, and particularly the government of Saskatchewan, are not themselves in a position to finance relief seed. Unless assistance is forthcoming from the federal government farmers either will have to procure their own seed, which means that many of them will not have seed, or will be compelled to go to the loan and mortgage companies for financing, a procedure which in my opinion would be a disaster in the extreme.
Last year a municipal secretary treasurer in my constituency showed me a note which had been sent to him by a mortgage company for a certain farmer to sign and return, for seed which they had supplied. The farmer signed the note at the rate of $1.70 per bushel for seed which he received at a time when wheat could be procured at the elevator for 74 cents per bushel.

Secondly, I wish to impress upon the government the need for haste in supplying the farmer with seed. Last year on March 11, a resolution was placed on the order paper giving advance notice of a seed grain bill.
On March 21 it was withdrawn from the order paper, and on March 23 it was reintroduced. The matter was debated on March 25, and was finally passed with senate amendments on April 4, fully a month after the farmers should have had the seed on their farms.
I am not saying this in any spirit of criticism; the thing has passed and there is no use in rehashing the matter, but I would remind the government that to all our requests for haste last year we were met constantly with the reply that the seed was at strategic points and could be given out on a few days' notice. We know now that in some districts the distribution was three or four weeks late. In one town in my own constituency the seed was distributed as late as May 8. Many farmers who lost their crops through rust and grasshoppers are absolutely convinced that they would have had some crop had they received their seed three or four weeks earlier. Let me draw to the attention of the government, particularly of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the fact that in six weeks from now the farmers will be getting ready for seeding and in eight weeks they will be on the land in some districts in Saskatchewan. At this time a declaration of policy ought to be made by persons in responsible positions.
The third matter I wish to place before the government is that facilities should be set up to enable farmers who have seed of a non-rust-resistant variety to exchange it for seed of a rust-resistant variety. Last fall it was stated repeatedly in western Canada that Thatcher wheat was being held throughout the west so that practically all farmers would be able to get it this spring. I hope that is so. If it is so, the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Finance ought to tell the people what facilities will be available, and how soon. Prompt action is necessary in this regard. If grasshoppers and rust are to be the menaces this summer that they were last summer it is very necessary that the farmers 
who have not rust-resistant seed should be able to exchange it on a bushel for bushel basis.
I urge the minister to make a statement to-day which will relieve the anxiety of the people in the drought areas of western Canada. All kinds of rumours are flying around. People write to tell me that they are sure they are not going to get seed. People are hearing different stories and they are not sure of the policy of the government. For instance. I came across the following statement in the Western Producer of February 2, 1939:
No Provision for Seed Yet
Taggart Charges Farmers did not Make Effort to Repay '38 Seed "There were too many farmers last fall who paid everyone else from their harvests and leit the rural municipality and the government holding the bag on seed gram loans.
"This year the municipality should let the individual know it is up to him to scratch up his own seed," said the Hon. J. G. Taggart, minister of agriculture, to the convention delegates of the central rural municipalities association meeting at Regina last -week. Out ot $18 000.000 loaned in Saskatchewan for seed, of which only $3,500,000 was not guaranteed by the dominion, farmers repaid only about $250,000," he said.
"So far," he added, "no arrangements ;have been made for 1939 seed grain financing.
That statement has caused widespread dismay among many farmers m my constituency, as well as in the surrounding constituencies. These farmers have not the seed necessary to put in a crop this year. Seeding is close at hand and many of these people are destitute. Their only hope of economic recovery is to obtain seed. With the prospects of _ a half decent crop they may be able to regain some measure of economic security.
I ask the government three questions. First, are they going to make provision for seed? Second, can there be some haste in the supplying of that seed so that it will be out in time? Third, will there be facilities to enable farmers to exchange non-rust-resistant varieties of seed for rust-resistant varieties, possibly on a reasonable basis such as bushel for bushel? I hope the government will make a statement through the Minister of Agriculture and assure the people of western Canada that this parliament and this government have not washed their hands of the matter, but are prepared to accept the responsibility which is really theirs of seeing that people who through no fault of their own have no seed will be given the necessary seed to enable them to rehabilitate themselves during the coming year.

Mr. V . G. MACDONALD (Brantford City) moved the second reading of Bill No. 20, respecting Central Finance Corporation and to change its name to Household Finance Corporation.

With reference to this bill, I should like to point out to the hon. member who moved the second reading that the principle involved in it was considered last session by the committee on banking and commerce. They made a report to this house, and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) introduced a bill of a general character which would govern these private companies' bills and regulate their rates to two per cent per month. This general bill was read the first time and laid
over. I should like to ask the minister whether he intends to introduce that bill again, and what is the present policy of the government this session regarding these small loan companies. In these times of depression the people cannot pay the high rates of interest charged by these companies. They have no credit with the banks because they have no security, with the result that small industrial workers are compelled to go to these loan companies, to pay fabulous sums of money, and often have to borrow from friends and relatives to help pay the Shylock interest rates on their loans.
I have received several hundred communications or ballots about an address made the other night on the radio by a fine citizen of Toronto, asking what we, as private members, are going to do about over-government and over-taxation and to help conditions for the workers. Other members must have received dozens of similar letters. Some of them are from the very people who are affected by these companies, and who have been forced out of their homes through the foreclosure of mortgages. I have seen the operations of one or two of these companies in the city I come from, and I am astonished that they come to this parliament to get charters and franchises and are given power to lend money on chattel mortgages, bills of sale and lien notes.
Not. by the wildest stretch of the imagination can these particular private bills of 1927, 1928 and 1929 be considered to be for the general advantage of Canada or within federal jurisdiction. Yet they come to this parliament, and they have got so many bills passed regarding this type of loan that I wonder what the provinces are doing, whether we have such a thing as property and civil rights in the provinces to give them control over this class of business. I should like to hear from the government what is to be its policy this session as to the general bill of 1938, which as I understand will provide some control as to rates over these companies when they are incorporated. Two per cent per month would be a universal rate, but an exoibitant one, when we consider how much money is hoarded in Canada, drawing no interest.
This matter was considered by the committee on banking and commerce of the senate, and a very valuable report was made last session by our own banking and commerce committee after a large number of prominent financial experts from the United States and elsewhere had gone most thoroughly into the matter. This bill might very well stand on the order paper until the government lays
Central Finance Corporation

down what is to be the policy regarding a general bill. Will the general bill of 1938 cover all these companies or not?
As regards this bill No. 20. I can assure the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) that, on account of my respect and esteem for him personally, I should like his bill to go through without any opposition as far as I am concerned, but I cannot see my way clear to support the second reading until the general principle has been laid down, because for twelve years I have opposed all these small loan companies and their rates and methods.
This bill is intended to change the name of the corporation to Household Finance Corporation. Of course they want to change the name. This company has been doing business right in the city I come from. I know of some of the loans which have been made to industrial workers there, and well they might want to change their names-these shark loan companies which are charging such a huge rate of interest. After the very conclusive evidence given by various experts, the time has come for Canada to stop granting any more of these charters, to cancel some of them, and to send these people to the provinces where they properly belong to get whatever charters the provinces will give them.
I may say so far as this particular bill goes that I was in the house when this company got the franchise, and I opposed the franchise. The term "shark loan company" was first applied by me in the discussion of that particular incorporation, which was away back in 1928 or 1929. We were then in opposition, and the opposition took very strong grounds against bills of this kind. It was charged by our late leader that these were matters concerning provincial rights, inasmuch as no doubt they have up here such influence as to take their charter out of the jurisdiction of the Interest Act and of the Loan Companies Act and of the Usury Act. These companies have taken themselves out of the limits of those three general statutes in order to come under federal jurisdiction, and have created a law unto themselves to charge anything they like; they are under no restrictions at all.
I can see no good reason why this bill should be read a second time. I wish to know from the Minister of National Revenue if he is going to introduce his bill of last session, which was recommended almost unanimously to the house by the committee on banking and commerce. If so, when will the bill be introduced, and will it provide some regulation of these companies?
I see that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is here to-night. I am glad to see

him here. For much of the time since I entered the house in 1921 he has been presiding most ably over the justice department, and in common with every other hon. member I wish to congratulate him on the thirty-fifth anniversary of his outstanding services to his. fellow man. He has been a wise custodian of public rights and of legislation for the benefit of the working people of this country, and is a statesman beloved by all. While the Minister of Justice is not supposed to give, as a minister, legal opinions to the house, I submit that since he is leading the government to-night, he ought to let us know what will be done with the report of the banking and commerce committee last session regarding the small loan companies, and whether some restrictions will check these small loans to workers.
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue); In the first place I should like to point out that this is a matter for the Department of Finance rather than for the Department of National Revenue. In the second place, I think it is usual for the government's policy on these matters to be announced from time to time as and when the occasion requires, and I am afraid I cannot give the hon. gentleman any further and better answer than that to-night-that the policy of the government in regard to this matter will be announced in due course. The immediate necessity is to decide what to do with this particular bill, and I understand that the sponsor of the bill is moving that it be referred to the banking and commerce committee, as is usual with measures of this kind.

This is a private bill dealing with only one company. Last year we had a number of these bills before the banking and commerce committee, and it was fairly well understood at the time that that committee would consider the principles underlying such bills and report to the House of Commons with a view to general legislation. I believe that there are evils in this small loan business which should be eliminated by this parliament and I am still of the opinion, as I was last year and the year before, that we should not now deal singly and separately with bills of this sort, but should again deal with the principle of the matter and endeavour to arrive at general legislation with regard to companies of this type. For that reason I am going to oppose this particular bill, though I would say that from the evidence produced before the committee there are companies in Canada which are not doing business in the manner

Central Finance Corporation
in which this company is; and while perhaps in opposing a bill with respect to a company which may be giving better service than most of the other companies, one may be doing something that appears to be discriminatory, nevertheless I hold that the principle is greater than the individual case and that we should try at the outset of this session to arrive at some general legislation dealing with all the small loan companies subject to our jurisdiction, adopting a principle upon which such general legislation can be based. For the reason I have stated, I am opposed to the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the committee on banking and commerce, of which I am a member, studied all these bills last year as well as in 1937. The house is aware that following prolonged deliberations and a careful study of the question the committee intended to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to bring in a general bill applicable to this company as to all similar ones.
On those occasions we were chiefly preoccupied with the rights of the provinces, for among the experts heard by the committee were representatives of Ontario, of Quebec, of Alberta and also, I believe, of one of the maritime provinces. The committee was unanimous in wishing to safeguard provincial rights. In fact that is what prolonged the discussions of last year. I therefore endorse the views of the two hon. members who preceded me, particularly my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) who is one of the most active members of the committee. Like him, I think we should either send the bill to the committee on banking and commerce or hold it until the Minister of Finance brings in a bill of general application.

I am opposed to the principle of the bill, but if it goes to a committee there is one thing which I think should be given serious consideration, and that is the advertisement that appears in newspapers and street cars under the name of this finance corporation, in which they say to the public something like this: "By special authority, rates of interest set by the dominion parliament." That is really saying to the public, "We have special authority to charge the rates we are charging, and therefore you are perfectly safe in doing business with us."
I do not believe that any company doing business as this company is should be allowed,
shall I say, to mislead the people in that way. My own view regarding these corporations is that instead of throwing a lifebuoy to people in times of stress they are really casting upon them an added weight which makes them sink deeper in the mire. It does not lift them out. I am voicing my protest against this legislation as I did last year.

We in this group are absolutely opposed to the bill. The rate of two per cent per month is exorbitant. We realize, of course, that that includes service charges, but we do not think that this parliament has the right to legislate with respect to service charges. That is a matter for the provincial legislature. Our view is therefore that if the government wish to pass further legislation they should enact that the rate of interest shall be, say, ten per cent per annum, and leave it to the provinces to cover the question of service charges. For that reason we are opposed to the bill.

I think the government should disclose its attitude towards this class of legislation. It is unfair to turn down this bill and the other one of the same type which is on the order paper, in the absence of some declaration to the house as to the policy of the government towards legislation of this sort.
It is known in this chamber that I have opposed this sort of legislation for many years -not that I oppose the requests of this and other companies, but I am opposed to the principle of establishing a rate of twenty-four or twenty-seven per cent per annum for loans, putting the imprimatur of parliament upon that rate. I have taken that position for twenty-seven years. The first time I expressed that view was in 1912 when I sought an amendment to the Interest Act and what was called the Money Lenders Act at that time, and I have consistently taken the same position ever since.
This, I believe, is the fourth session that this and similar companies have been before parliament, but during the last two or three years, particularly last year, there has been a disposition on the part of the government to introduce general legislation covering the matter, and this company and the other company mentioned in Bill No. 21 held back for a certain time in the expectation that the general law would pass. Had the general law passed, they were not so particular except for a change of name or something of that kind; but some of these bills have been prepared so that they may have this power to charge two per cent per month in the absence of general legislation.
Central Finance Corporation

I suggest that the government ought to come forward frankly and say whether or not they are going to introduce again the legislation which was the result of two sessions of hearings before the banking and commerce committee of this house and also in one year before the banking committee of another place. The government should frankly declare its position on the matter.
There are two classes of borrowers that patronize this sort of loan company-and these companies themselves so inform me. There is what I would call the class A borrower, whom I shall describe in a moment, and this embraces the larger number. There is also the class B borrower, the smaller class. The class A borrower is the salaried person or some person with a known and fixed income, who temporarily has suffered reverse through illness in the family or perhaps some serious operations that call for extraordinary expenditure-the sort of person who the company knows is good. That class of borrower must pay the two per cent per month which really is applicable only to the second class. The second class comprises those who find themselves in difficulties through improvidence or carelessness, or, as often happens, probably through playing the race track or the stock market. It is not fair that the class A borrowers, who they know are good, with whom the records and evidence showed there was only a fraction of one per cent loss, a fraction so small that we were all surprised at it, should be penalized because there is a larger risk on the more improvident and careless borrowers whom I have included in class B.
For that reason I have taken the stand that we need in Canada facilities to enable the bona fide salaried man, with an assured income, a position and good character, to get money in cases of emergency on much easier terms, say seven per cent or something of the kind. It is true that one of the banks has already started a personal loan department. I believe that the government-I say this to the government as an institution, and not in any critical sense-might very well call in the bankers and see if they would not take up that line of business as a part of their duty to the country. I know they do not wish to do it, because it is small business, not very profitable, it may be; and perhaps they consider it a little beneath their dignity. But there ought to be provided in the urban districts the kind of legislation that we have in the rural credits act. Unfortunately the rural credits act, passed I believe in 1925, does not function, I think through lack of administrative interest in it on the part of this and previous governments. But this class
[Mr. Stevens.)
of legislation, properly enforced, and with the support and interest of the government, might very well become an extremely useful form of assistance to needy borrowers.
Having said that much I want to make it clear that in spite of all my opposition to these measures, which at times has been definite and perhaps heated, I do not think parliament should just crowd them out or refuse to consider them. In justice and fairness we must listen to the requests of any body of people who are within the law. These people are within the law. They are within their right in coming to parliament, and I am not going to oppose the second reading of these bills. But I want to place on record my attitude and views in connection with this matter and to urge upon the government that either before these bills have second reading or before they are finally disposed of we have the assurance that the government will during this session introduce such public measures as may be necessary to deal with this very important question.

These bills are a pair of twins, and each year they have been up I have registered my opposition to them. I have been one of those who advocated the lowering of interest rates and urged that the dominion government take the lead in that respect. We have now pretty well got that, and I do not see how we can open the other door and allow private corporations or any particular group of people to charge interest at the rates these people expect to get. I know a man who this summer paid $500, all but $40, for a piano, and he was not able to raise that $40, so he lost his piano and his money, with merely the promise that perhaps he would get a better rate next time. I have nothing but contempt for a corporation which, finding a man up against it in his endeavour to hold property of some kind, professes to be his friend and lends him money at a rate of interest that it is impossible for him to pay. That is selfishness run wild.
I have been asked why I was so strongly opposed to these corporations. It is because I have seen these people completely up against it and unable to pay the piper that I determined that if I ever got the opportunity I would hit this thing as hard as I could. If this bill goes to the committee it is all right, but if it is to go through now I shall oppose it as strongly as I can.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I think we all recognize
that it is on the motion for second reading that the principle of a bill is decided upon, not in committee; that is where the details are supposed to be dealt with. I believe it is two years since the government promised us that we should have general legislation on this matter. Only this afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was urging upon the house the responsibility of the government for carrying forward the affairs of the country. In this instance the government is distinctly responsible. And while, as my colleague behind me has said, I do not like voting against a particular measure in order to stop the general practice to which objection is taken, I see no other way of stopping it than by opposing it at this stage. The responsibility then is not upon the house; it is fairly placed upon the government, and they can bring down their general legislation.
It is all very well to say that this company has come in good faith to parliament; of course it has. Any group of men can come to parliament with various proposals, but it is for the house to say whether or not the principle underlying them is good. I do not see what else we can do at this stage than oppose the principle of the bill. We hope that before very long the government will introduce general legislation covering this matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I hesitate to speak on this question, as the minister in charge of this branch of government business is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) who to-night is unavoidably absent. I may however remind the house that if this bill is defeated the situation will remain as it is to-day. If I remember correctly, when a similar bill was discussed last year it was pointed out that whatever may be the demerits of the carrying on of business by such corporations, if this bill be adopted it will constitute a great improvement on the present condition. I am not a member of the banking and commerce committee and I do not know what took place there last year. I do remember that when the bill came back it could not be put through because time did not permit. I agree largely with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). I am opposed to anybody, corporation or individual, charging an exorbitant rate of interest. I am free to confess that in my early years I was a victim of that sort of thing. But I do not see what harm would be done by again sending this bill to the committee, if it is really an improvement on the present situation. There it can be discussed and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) can be heard as to whether or not there will be a general act introduced covering this field of activity. As to that I am not in a position to make any statement on the part of the government.
Under the circumstances I would vote to send the bill to the committee, without binding myself to support it if it is reported back to the house, particularly should it have the effect of making permanent a situation to which we all object.

I am opposed to this bill in principle. I believe the original mistake was made some years ago when these companies were incorporated and given special rights beyond the provisions of the Money-Lenders Act. It is very true that these two bills have been before the banking and commerce committee for the last two sessions, but it does not reflect very much credit upon us as a parliament that at this
92S
Central Finance Corporation

session we should be asked, by way either of special or of general legislation, to authorize a rate of interest of two per cent per month. If that is the only message we have for the people of Canada we cannot seriously complain if the people say it is too bad for us.
During the discussion last year we heard a great deal about the Russell Sage Foundation in the United States, which I understand is a very estimable institution and which has done a great deal of good work. But the remedies suggested by that foundation have not rectified the situation in the United States, and, that being the case, we can hardly expect them to meet with greater success here. I think we might well go to the banking institutions, which for a long period of years have received many concessions from the people of this country, and say that they should give greater consideration to this kind of business. I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that the banks do not care to handle this business, but I believe our banking institutions could not make a greater contribution to the solution of the problems that confront us than by catering to and serving the people who ordinarily would be customers of institutions of this kind. I believe our banks are prepared now, as they have never been prepared in the past, for business of this kind. In the last three years they have lent some $24,000,000 under the home improvement plan at a discount rate of 31 per cent, and I understand that so far the losses have been less than one per cent. I was talking with a banker who had lent a very considerable sum of money under this plan, and he expressed surprise that the business had turned out so satisfactorily. Not a single loan was in arrears; not a single dollar had been lost, and he said, " We of the banking profession are overlooking a very profitable field for investment. If we did cater to that field we would have a profitable outlet for funds that we have difficulty in investing at the present time."
I noticed also that in the deliberations last year, as the hon. member for Kootenay East mentioned, there was an attempt to distinguish between the kinds of borrowers. There was likewise an attempt to distinguish between the companies doing this business, with one referring to another as money sharks and loan sharks. For the life of me I cannot see any distinguishing feature between companies that charge 24 per cent or more. There is a remedy in the Money-Lenders Act, where interest rates are specified. If some detail is lacking in that act at present let us put teeth into that statute and meet the situation by

prosecuting those who are profiting through the difficulties in which unfortunate people find themselves.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, it seems quite obvious that there is a great deal of opposition to this bill. There is no doubt, as the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party has said, that if we send this bill to the banking and commerce committee we will adopt the principle. If there is one thing in which I believe the people of this country feel the government should give some lead it is this question of the curtailment of the interest that these companies charge. For three or four years the newspapers have been full of the discussion which has taken place both in the banking and commerce committee and in this house. I suggest that this bill be held up in order to permit the government to bring in some measure that will cure these evils. Or the banking and commerce committee might take up the question and recommend suitable legislation to the house. Surely we cannot pass this bill again and endorse the principle of usury which is practised throughout this country.
Mr. J. T. THORSON (Selkirk). A year ago I spoke on a bill which was introduced respecting this company. The subject had been carefully studied by the standing committee on banking and commerce, which was very greatly divided in its opinions. The objection which I raised a year ago, and which I repeat now, was that if we passed this bill authorizing a monthly charge of two per cent, we would do so under our authority to deal with interest rates. We have by the Money-Lenders Act set a maximum rate of interest of twelve per cent per annum, and it would be a mistake on the part of this parliament to give its imprimatur to a higher rate of interest than that. The objection which I took a year ago was to the lumping of the total charge. I suggested that we might, in the general legislation which was before us, require that the rate of interest, as such, should be stated; that it should not exceed the rate of interest now set forth in the Money-Lenders Act, and that the balance of the charge, other than interest, might be left to the provincial jurisdiction.
This of course is a bill amending the charter of a dominion corporation, and the objection which I have to the bill in its present form is that it lumps the interest part of the charge with that part of the charge which is not interest. That, Mr. Speaker, is in my opinion

Central Finance Corporation
objectionable. The rate of interest should be specified as not exceeding the rate now set by the Money-Lenders Act.
As the bill stands I shall feel it my duty to vote against the motion for second reading.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that the government should entertain this whole question very seriously, and bring down legislation for discussion in the house. It seems to me that we have no right to stand at the back of those who would leech on the misfortunes of our people, and that is what these bills amounts to.
The suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) is very timely, and I find myself quite in agreement with the idea that the chartered banks could take this duty upon themselves. They may want to be high-brow about their work, but they are the manipulators of the currency and credit of this country. They are allowed to conduct their business as such, and this is directly one part of that feature of their work. It seems to me that in time to come if we are to leave the chartered banks in their present positions we shall ask them to undertake a great deal more work, not less, on behalf of the people.
I am definitely opposed to the principle of these bills.
Mr. A. MacG. YOUNG (Saskatoon): Mr. Speaker, last year when this or a similar bill was before the house it was sent to the committee on banking and commerce, where I understand it was given a great deal of consideration. I doubt whether if it went there this year any new facts could be elicited either for or against the bill, and it seems to me almost like a waste of time to send it to the committee again this year. No doubt there are persons who require or desire loans, in a small way, and who are prepared to pay a rate of interest higher than the banks charge. But so far as I am concerned I am definitely opposed to high rates of interest anywhere.
When this country pays above two per cent interest, I think it is too high. When the provinces pay a little more than that, perhaps, I think it is too high. When we are called upon by our banks to pay six, seven or eight per cent, I think it is too high. But when we are asked to pay two per cent per month-well, Mr. Speaker, I just simply cannot support any bill which follows a principle of that kind. I intend to vote against the motion for second reading.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the committee on banking and commerce it was my duty to spend a good many days listening to the evidence concerning these small loan companies. I hold no brief for them; I have never had to use them, and I hope I never will. But there are one or two points I should like to draw to the attention of the house.
I do not think it is quite fair to put down the rate of interest at twenty-four per cent per year. A man borrows $50 for a month, we will say, and at the end of the month he pays it back, the transaction having cost him one dollar. For thirty years I was in the habit of borrowing money from the banks, while carrying out my business as a farmer. I never paid	less	than	eight per	cent peryear, and in	the	very	nature of	things Inever could pay back in less than eight months. So	that	any	money I	borrowed
from the bank cost me six per cent, because I could not pay it back in less time.
There is this further point to consider: These small loan companies lend their own money, or money which first of all they have to borrow. The bank does not do that; it creates what	it loans,	and the	procedure
costs it nothing. It creates costless credit, and I think that is an important point for consideration.
Then, there is this further matter for consideration: When a small loan company forecloses on a client, in the nature of things it is a public exhibition. The security is put out on the street for all the neighbours to see. When a bank forecloses it is a silent, secret process. Not even a man's wife may know that her husband's security has been foreclosed. As a matter of fact the bank already has the security in its safe, and all that happens is that it stays in the safe and does not come out.
As I have said, I hold no brief for the small loan companies. But I was struck during the time I spent in the committee on banking and commerce with the treatment which these companies received. One might think that in a sense they were criminals. Of course a loan shark is a criminal, but I do not think we can say that a company conducting business at the rate of two per cent per month is committing a crime. However they received no respect whatsoever, while on the other hand the banks receive all the respect in the world.

Central Finance Corporation

I do not think that is fair. I believe that for every man who has been foreclosed and put out of business by a small loan company there are a hundred who have been put out of business and had their security foreclosed by our banks. That is all I wish to say on the subject, but I thought it my duty to bring these few points to the attention of the house.
I repeat that I have no brief whatever for the small loan company. I never have used one, and I hope I never will have to.

Mr. Speaker, first I should like to
express my appreciation of the very kind remarks made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) about myself. I may say that I hold him in the highest regard and esteem. He was mayor of the city of Toronto for a number of years, I believe it was eight, during which time he gained the respect of the people of that city. Subsequently he was elected to this house, where he has gained the respect and admiration of all members. I am pleased to know that he will not support this bill for personal reasons. Far be it from me to want any hon. member, no matter how kindly he may feel toward me personally, to vote for any measure merely for personal reasons.
The hon. member for Broadview and other hon. members referred to the loan shark. In presenting this bill to the house for second reading I cannot express too strongly how I feel toward the loan shark. These people have been bleeding those who could not afford to pay. They have taken the small pittances of many working men, women and girls in order to swell their own coffers. I think all hon. members will agree with me when I say that something must be done to curb the activities of the loan shark. One hon. member has said, I believe it was the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), that during this last year the newspapers have been demanding action by this government in connection with the curbing of loan sharks. As he and other hon. members know, last year the banking and commerce committee was requested specifically to deal with this matter. Numerous hearings were held and many witnesses were called from various provinces and from different states of the republic to the south. I have not the report before me, but I recall that a representative of the attorney general's office of Alberta, I believe it was the deputy attorney

general, appeared before the committee to advocate that the loan shark evil be curbed.
To-night the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) stated that in his opinion some of these loan companies were not as bad as other so-called respectable institutions. He contended that they were less drastic in their methods than some of our financial institutions. Whether this evil is in the form of a great financial institution, a chartered loan company or an individual, it must be curbed. These activities cannot be allowed to continue. The newspapers of the country, led by that great national paper the Globe and Mail, have advocated in the strongest terms that action should be taken immediately by parliament. I recall reading an editorial in that paper toward the end of last session advocating that action be taken immediately, and that if it were too late, then the government should bring in a bill at the next session.
Numerous speakers this evening have said that legislation should be brought down by the government. We are in the early days of the session and I agree that legislation should be brought down covering not only loan companies that come here for their charters, but those which receive charters from the various provinces. The legislation should control all companies and individuals.
I hope my position in this matter will be understood. I want to control the rates of interest charged and to prevent excessive rates and unscrupulous methods being followed by individuals and corporations. Hon. members will remember that last spring a number of prosecutions took place in the Toronto courts. Certain individuals and companies were accused of charging not two per cent per month, but, if my memory serves me correctly, ninety-seven per cent per month. Evidence was presented last year to the committee on banking and commerce that exorbitant rates of more than one thousand per cent had been charged.
Shame.

No wonder an hon. member says "shame." I join with him in saying "shame." That is the sort of practice which should be curbed. The incorporation of this company will be one method of preventing the charging of excessive rates of interest. It is one method of controlling the rates charged and the various activities of these companies.

Seed Grain-Mr. Perley
