speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Dunning for committee of supply.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was about to associate myself with the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) in his request that the government should make a statement with respect to the distribution of seed grain in those areas in the west which happen to require it for the spring seeding. The hon. member recited to the house what had taken place last year when the bill to provide seed grain was before the house, and how we facilitated the passing of the measure. Hon. members will recall that when the house was in committee I was asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) for certain information. The minister suggested that we should discontinue asking for information and facilitate the passing of the bill. We were told that we would later have an opportunity of getting the necessary information.
Although we facilitated the passing of that bill in good time, there was delay, as referred to by the hon. member for Weyburn, in the distribution of seed in some parts of Saskatchewan. I know of districts where seed was not delivered until after May 10. When it was not rust-resistant wheat that was seeded it was affected by the rust and subjected to the grasshopper infestation.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: May 10 is a good time.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
It was very late for last year. At Easter time when we were home, seeding conditions were good and wheat should have been in the ground. It is estimated by those who are in a position to estimate that the loss sustained by the province, and producers in particular, owing to the lateness of the seeding, amounted to thirty to forty million dollars. The question is already agitating the minds of the western farmer; for we know that in many places it has been taken up at conventions and other gatherings of farmers. I have here a report in the Regina Daily Star of January 31:
Outlook for Provision of Seed Grain Gloomy.
No plans yet but late Announcement may be made.	.
Every bit of evidence on the question that can be picked up around the parliament buildings-
In Regina.
-points to a tough year for the Saskatchewan farmer who faces the coming crop season without seed.
71492-59J
Official statements on any plans for the distribution of relief seed the government may have in mind are singularly lacking. Honourable J. G. Taggart, minister of agriculture, from his seat on the floor of the legislative assembly room has bluntly stated the government is not in a position to make an announcement.
A little earlier than that, on January 26, is a report in the same paper of a request for early distribution of seed grain. The report is as follows:
Directors of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, headed by J. J. McGurran, secretary, met members of the government Wednesday to discuss resolutions passed at a recent meeting in Regina.
The directors asked the government to "immediately evolve" a policy of seed distribution, with provision for early delivery, with the price on a parity with market prices, plus "reasonable" distribution cost; that rust-resisting types be distributed at the same price the wheat board sells to millers, grades considered.
That shows, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of the west are concerned and anxious, especially when what took place last year is fresh in their memories.
I might also remind hon. members that on January 27 of this year I asked the Minister of Finance if the government was giving any consideration to this matter and if representations had been made to them by the provincial government or any others in the west with respect to it; and on page 380 of Hansard the Minister of Finance stated that no request of which he had any knowledge had come to the government. In respect to that I was informed about January 15 or 16, by a member of a delegation that was in Ottawa meeting with the government, though not on this matter, that they believed that the Saskatchewan government had made a request for assistance in the amount of three and a half million dollars towards guaranteeing the banks, the province and the municipalities for distribution of seed this spring. I believe that my informant was a responsible person, and in a position to know; for he is associated with one of the largest grainhandling concerns in western Canada. The amount he mentioned would, I think, be adequate. It is about half of what was required last year for wheat alone. The present price at Fort William is about sixty-five cents as compared with $1.45 last year, and when one also considers that the area is not nearly as great this year, that amount should certainly be adequate.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: That is not half of what they had last year.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
For wheat, I think.
Seed Grain-Mr. Perley

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: They had twenty-one million dollars last year.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Yes, but that was for all grains.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Most of it was for wheat.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Well, I believe that the minister, who knows as well as I do the area which requires assistance this year, will agree that at the present price three and a half million dollars would be ample. I think farmers would be very well pleased if they heard that this government is prepared to guarantee that amount.
I think we should have had a report with respect to the distribution last year and who was responsible for the delay. We know that the provincial government and the wheat board have said that they were not responsible, and I have no doubt this government will make the same answer. Certainly the municipalities were not to blame, because they had their estimates in in good time, and it is due to this house and to western Canada to know where the responsibility lies.
Last year, speaking on this matter, I made the statement with respect to price that the wheat could have been delivered at SI.10 per bushel. I am still of that opinion. I followed the conversion of the option into the cash grain, and I was not refuted in my argument, which I think proved to be correct, that wheat could have been delivered to the farmer at SI.10.
I am very much disappointed with the price at which seed oats and barley were delivered last year. I regard 674 cents to the farmer as very unreasonable. A lot of the oats required for seed were imported from the United States at a time when the market in the United States was 304 cents for May oats, 42 cents for cash oats, and in the spring of the year the option never got above 33 cents. Allowing for the freight to North Portal and the further freight to the interior of the province where the oats were required, they could have been delivered at around 56 cents. It has never been satisfactorily explained why the charge to the farmer was 674 cents.
It seems to me that this year wheat should be delivered as the hon. member for Wey-burn has stated, on an exchange of bushel for bushel, a bushel of non rust-resisting wheat for a bushel of rust-resisting wheat. That is only fair, especially when we consider what the farmer paid last year. Certainly if the farmer is not in a position to exchange, and has to purchase, it should be delivered to him at the going price on the Winnipeg exchange.
{Mr. Perley.]
Taking the cash wheat at Fort William at 65 cents, that would net the farmer at the initial point about 55 to 60 cents, which would include the freight and the cost of distribution.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: Freight both ways?

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: No, not at all. The minister knows I did not mean that. He knows enough about the business to understand I am referring to freight from one point in the province to the point where it is required.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: May I just point out, in order not to have the matter misrepresented, that if you want seed grain in a locality there is in all probability no seed there; there is no wheat there; and if the wheat is shipped to a central elevator and then shipped back to another elevator you have freight both ways on it.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
The minister knows quite well, I think, what I was saying and the interpretation to put on the language I was using. The cost of wheat at the elevator in which it is at the present time and what the board has paid for it would be 80 cents. The board is selling that wheat to the trade at 65 cents Fort William. When you take off the freight to Fort William and the cost of commission and so on, it would be about 50 cents in the interior where it is at the present time. Then add to that the freight which is required to take it from the place where it now is in the interior to the place where it is required for seed. I will allow 10 cents for that, 5 cents for distribution costs, and 50 cents, which is more than adequate, as the initial price, and we have 65 cent wheat. 1 think it is the duty of this government to see that the distribution this spring takes place at a fair and reasonable price to the producer requiring that seed.
The minister should also be very careful to see that the cost of the coarse grain seed shall be fair and reasonable. Oats have been delivered in the northern parts of the province at the elevators at from 11 to 15 cents a bushel, and of course there would be storage and cost of shipping from one point in the interior to the Other point requiring the product. I submit the government should see to it that the oats this year are delivered at not more than 30 cents a bushel, instead of at 67 cents as happened last year.
I do not think it is necessary to delay the house at this time. The minister is well acquainted with the facts and he should be prepared to make a statement and to introduce the necessary bill as soon as possible. Considering the experience of last spring,

Seed Grain-Mr. Gardiner
more questions will be asked and more information will be required than was the case last year. With the experience of last year, and knowing what happened as regards delay and cost and so on, I suggest that this government should undertake the supervision and distribution as well as the control of price and deliveries this year. The hon. member for Weyburn indicated the importance of the matter and I think the position of the western producer at the present time should receive serious consideration. He is very much concerned because this is the 14th of February and it takes quite a time to distribute the seed and clean it. The farmers should know where they stand and what will be done. When the bill comes before the house I shall be pleased to do all I can to facilitate its passage, and I trust that we shall receive a reasonable amount of information regarding the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
The question of seed grain and
seed grain supplies for the different provinces has been under consideration from year to year, at least ever since I have been in public life. It was one of the standing questions in 1914 and has been in quite a number of years from that date down to the present time. Last year I had applications from every province in Canada except Nova Scotia and British Columbia for assistance from the federal government in order to provide seed grain. When these applications came from Quebec, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and other provinces we gave the same answer to all-that the provision of seed grain to farmers in the different provinces of Canada has always been looked upon as a provincial responsibility and has always been taken care of by the provincial governments. The matter of financing has occasionally been assisted in by the federal government, but as regards the distribution of seed grain and the responsibility for securing seed grain for farmers, the provincial governments have taken care of that from one end of Canada to the other.
The question of seed grain is an annual problem in the province of Quebec, for example. As I understand it, year after year the government of Quebec has to go to Alberta or somewhere else in western Canada and purchase seed oats and have it shipped to the province of Quebec where it is distributed to the farmers, the cost being, I presume, charged to the farmers. On a number of occasions we have assisted in financing the provision of seed in the three western provinces, perhaps to a greater degree in Saskatchewan than in any other province, and last year
we were required to supply more in the way of finances in order to take care of the seed grain situation in that province than in any previous year. There had to be found, in order to purchase seed and pay for its distribution last year, the sum of 821,000,000. Between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 of that amount was provided by mortgage companies; about $18,000,000 was provided by municipalities. They borrowed the amount from the banks. About $3,500,000 was guaranteed by the province without any federal guarantee, and the other $14,500,000 was guaranteed by the government of Canada.
I believe it was the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) who said that the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, in a statement recently, said that only $250,000 of that amount was collected back last year. I think that is approximately correct so that there is still outstanding on the lands of Saskatchewan, as a result of loans made last year for seed grain, something in the neighbourhood of $21,000,000, in addition to all that had been lent in the years preceding that in order to provide seed grain.
It will be seen, therefore, that this is not a matter that can be considered lightly; it is not a question that we are asked to consider for the first time; and it is not a matter about which the farmers of Saskatchewan have to my knowledge been making any considerable complaint. I do not believe there are any considerable number of fa'mers in Saskatchewan, or Alberta, or Manitoba, who do not realize that somebody, somewhere, has been putting forth a sustained effort in order to make it possible for them to reseed their lands from year to year. There are no farmers in Canada who appreciate more thoroughly what has been done by the peopl of all Canada, and particularly what was done last year by the people of all Canada, in order to make possible the seeding of the land than the farmers of Saskatchewan.
In regard to the distribution of the seed, I do not think that any government ever undertook a task so great, of a similar nature, as the task that was undertaken last year by the government of Saskatchewan in the distribution of $21,000,000 worth of seed to the farmers of that province, and I can only say that if the worst that any hon. member of this house can say in discussing the matter now is that some farmer did not get seed until May 8th or 10th there is not very much reason for criticism with respect to the distribution of that seed. I venture to say that there is just about as much wheat seeded around the 10th of May in the average year in Saskatchewan as is seeded about any date.
Seed Grain-Mr. Gardiner

If the seed was available by the 8th or 10th of May to all the farmers of Saskatchewan then the task was very much more efficiently carried out than I myself thought it was.
There is another way of looking at it. Had there been anything in the way of neglect on the part of the government or of anyone who was associated with the distribution of this seed grain, if one were to examine the records, one would expect to find that the acreage seeded last year was very much lower than otherwise would have been the case. But when we examine the record of the acreage seeded in Saskatchewan last year we find that it was only slightly below that of the previous year-less than one million acres below the previous year and less than one million acres below the previous ten year average. So I do not think any considerable criticism can be made with regard to the distribution of seed last year.
Coming to the present year I may point out that before November 21 last, the government of Saskatchewan made a very thorough survey of the situation existing in that province, and they indicated to the government of Canada the production of wheat per acre in the different municipalities. At the same time they called the attention of the farmers of Saskatchewan to the necessity of providing themselves with their own seed as far as possible for the coming spring. I should go back even further than that. Earlier than November the government of Saskatchewan came to this government and asked for assistance to keep the farmers through this winter. They said they would require $9,000,000 to buy food and clothing for the farmers of the province and their families who were without crops last year, and also to provide some feed grain in areas where there was none. The government of Canada made that money available to Saskatchewan, and at the time it was made available the provincial government made an announcement to the people of Saskatchewan. They said: The federal government have provided us with funds with which to maintain the farmers throughout the winter. It will be absolutely unnecessary for any farmer, in order to keep himself through the winter, to sell any of his seed grain. And because we are going to provide the wherewithal to live through the winter and feed the live stock we expect every farmer who had a crop of two or three or four bushels to the acre as a result of last year's seeding to retain that grain in his bins in order to be able to seed his crop this spring. I know from the few letters I am receiving to-day from the different parts of Saskatchewan as compared with what we
IMr. Gardiner.]
received in previous years that the great majority-I would say 99 per cent of the farmers of Saskatchewan-have carried out these instructions and have the seed grain, if they grew it last year.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext: What about those who have not?

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
I do not intend to say anything to-night, and I hope no other member will say anything, that would tend to undo any of the good work that was done by the government of Saskatchewan in seeing to it that that seed grain was kept in the bins until next spring. We can argue ourselves black in the face as to the cost of wheat laid down at an elevator, but anyone who ever had anything to do with them knows that elevator companies-and the pools are no exception-do what every other business concern does. When they buy grain at a certain point and that grain is supposed to go to Fort William-and if it went there it would have to be shipped back to any locality to provide seed-nine times out of ten the farmer has to pay a considerable part of the costs on the grain both ways, no matter where it was loaded or was unloaded.
And there is another thing to be considered. On grain for export, either east or west, there is a special freight rate. But there are no special rates for shipping grain north and south across Saskatchewan. If you ship grain from Melfort in northern Saskatchewan to the southern part of the province it costs practically as much in many instances as it would to ship it all the way from the centre of Saskatchewan to the seaboard. In view of those facts it is impossible to stand up here and try to figure what the price of grain is going to be, delivered to a farmer, after it has once been in an elevator. Any man who has had any practical experience knows that he cannot speak in generalities about the cost. So what the government of Saskatchewan is saying to the farmers of Saskatchewan to-day is this: You can get that seed grain cheaper than anyone else. In spite of what has been said to-night I venture to say that there is not one farm in Saskatchewan to-day that is more than twenty or twenty-five miles away from seed grain, and I think I know the province fairly well; I have driven over it all.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
What can
they use for money? The seed may be procurable, but they need some assistance in financing.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
The farmers in Saskatchewan are like farmers anywhere else. I know that as far as the farmers in the

Seed Grain-Mr. Coldwell
community in which I live are concerned, if there are farmers who have seed grain their neighbours are not going to have a great deal of difficulty in getting it and getting it into the ground, unless someone starts to do something that in the end will make the cost a great deal more than it would be if done in a spirit of cooperation. By stirring up too much discussion of this question at this time we are not helping the farmers of Saskatchewan, but are making it more costly for them to get the seed grain that they are going to require to seed their crops.
Past experience has shown that few if any farmers in Saskatchewan have ever gone without seed grain, and that they get the seed grain most cheaply when they are able to obtain it without its being put in elevators and taken out again. It will be found that if and when and where this seed grain is required there will be no serious difficulty experienced in getting it. On the other hand I hope that no one, provincially, municipally or otherwise, is doing anything which will leave the impression that seed grain is to be supplied this spring no matter what anyone may do with the grain he had last fall. I think seed grain will be found for those who are in absolute need of it. Some way or other money will be found to pay for it, but the announcement of definite methods for going out to get say $3,500,000 worth of seed grain at the present time to be distributed in Saskatchewan or anywhere else is not going to help the farmers; and it would cost this government, or someone in Canada, perhaps the provincial government or the municipalities, a great deal more than to proceed as the provincial government is proceeding to-day. We are fully informed regarding the situation in Saskatchewan, and the Saskatchewan government is fully informed. The farmers also are pretty fully informed regarding the situation, as some of the quotations from the press have indicated. If we allow the matter to be dealt with by the province it will be handled just as effectively as it has always been, and the acreage which should be seeded to wheat in Saskatchewan this year will be seeded, as it has been in the past.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Before the minister sits
down perhaps he will permit me to ask two or three questions. He says there is not a farmer in Saskatchewan who is not within twenty-five miles of a supply of seed grain. Does he say that seed is all of a rust-resistant variety?

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
No, I would not say
that is rust-resistant wheat. There is not
rust-resistant wheat enough to seed all the farms in western Canada this year. And of course there are some people who would not seed rust-resistant varieties of wheat that some others are seeding at the present time. There are some farmers who would not sow particular kinds of wheat about which there is a great deal of discussion. After all, we get rust about once in ten years on an average, and there are some people who will sow varieties of wheat that are not called rust-resistant because of the higher yields they get with what they consider better varieties.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Can the minister give us
any information as to who is holding the great bulk of the Thatcher wheat that is available for seed? Is it in the hands of elevator companies or of the wheat board?

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
Order. I would remind
the hon. member that we are not in committee. This is not the proper time for questions of this kind.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF SEED GRAIN IN WESTERN PROVINCES-STATEMENT OF MR. T. C. DOUGLAS
speechtext:
I do not think anyone in this chamber desires to make things more difficult either for the minister and his department or for the farmers of western Canada than it is going to be in the near future. But I do think that to-night the minister has placed rather an optimistic picture before us. He says he is sure there are farmers who will have seed available for their neighbours who lack it, but it seems to me the difficulty is that unquestionably there were many thousands of acres last year that were seeded to marquis wheat on which no crops were cut, and where much of the wheat that was cut was of very low grade and probably very poor germinative quality. Consequently in those areas, if farmers are to be able to seed their land and look forward to the reaping of a crop, better seed will have to be provided than is in their immediate vicinity. The minister said he did not believe there was sufficient rust-resistant wheat in the province or the provinces to meet all the needs. I think that is probably true, but I believe there is at least a very large amount, which may cover a greater acreage than I have personal knowledge about at the moment. The minister ought to be, and I expect he is, much better informed than I am on that particular score.
Reference was made to the fact that collections on account of the seed that was supplied last year and in previous years were very bad. I think that is true, and the reason, of course, is the condition of the country, the poor crops, the series of crop failures, the low grades and the insufficient price. I know many
Seed Grain-Mr. Coldwell

members of parliament from eastern constituencies think the eighty cent price adopted by the government this year provided an amount sufficient to meet the requirements of the wheat producer. Well, I do not propose to go into that question to-night, because on the estimates and elsewhere we will have opportunities to take up that aspect of the problem. I would say, however, that if hon. members will read the very interesting report of the proceedings of the conference on markets for western farm products, which I believe was circulated to all members by the Manitoba government, they will find a very authoritative analysis of the cost of producing a bushel of wheat in western Canada on various types of land and various sizes of farms over average periods of years. They will see that according to Professor Hope, who made the analysis- and whose figures were not disputed even by representatives of the grain exchange who were there-the Saskatchewan farmer required an average farm price of approximately ninety cents a bushel. The eighty cent price is on the basis of Fort William, and from that you must subtract fifteen, sixteen, eighteen or more cents a bushel to see what the farmer actually gets.

A great deal of land was ready for crop but, as I said at the outset, many thousands of acres of marquis and other varieties of wheat that were not rust-resistant were not cut last autumn, and the farmers who did not cut that grain will have no seed this spring. This is something I want to present to the government. I hope that in setting the price of wheat they will deal fairly with all the parties concerned. We had several intimations from the minister to-night that this is a matter primarily for the provinces. I should like the minister to make a statement of the services rendered by the dominion Department of Agriculture which could not be rendered by the departments of the various provinces. This question of where the responsibility rests is becoming more difficult of definition year by year. There is an increasing number of farmers who are convinced that there is a duplication as between the federal Department of Agriculture and the provinces. This belief is becoming more widespread year by year. We will soon be taking up the estimates and after looking

Supply-Agriculture-Administration
through them I must say that with the exception of a few items, I cannot see anything that is not handled already by the provincial governments.
The question is being asked as to what plan the departments of agriculture, both federal and provincial, have to further the welfare of agriculture in this dominion. Is the minister working towards the objective of bettering the condition of agriculture? The following statement by Great Britain's minister of agriculture appeared the other day in the Western Producer:
The objective for agriculture. Sir Reginald says, should be to secure a level of prices for farm products that will enable the farmer to conduct his operations in a scientific and efficient manner, to pay wages for his help that correspond to wages received by other skilled labour and to earn for himself a reasonable standard of living. That is the objective he set before the farmers of the empire.
The federal Department of Agriculture in cooperation with the provinces should map out a plan with that definite objective in view. This question has been raised ever since confederation, ever since the departments were formed. The condition of agriculture, both in the east and in the west, is such that some plan with a definite objective should be worked out. I feel like saying that I hesitate to give my approval to voting over nine and a half millions for the Department of Agriculture unless I am satisfied that that department is rendering a special service that warrants this expenditure. After all, if the dominion meets its obligations that money must be drawn from the provinces. The question in my mind is whether those estimates should be prevented from passing and the money left in the provinces. The question is whether the provinces could not administer this vote to better advantage.
Motion agreed to. and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

Administration service-
1. Departmental administration, $120,005.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it, this item raises the whole question of the activities of the Department of Agriculture, the manner in which they are conducted and the organization of the department. Some two years ago the announcement was made in the columns of the press that certain changes were to be made in the organization of the Department of Agriculture. Later on the minister was asked what those changes were to be and he requested that the answer should be allowed to wait
71492-60 i
until a certain item came up. Unfortunately that item did not come up in that year until the dying days of the session, and nothing was heard of the changes which were to be brought about. Last year the question was again asked as to the changes which were to be made and the additions to the service, if any, and the minister did make a short statement. In my opinion that statement was neither satisfactory nor at all complete. I ask the minister to give the committee and the country a real explanation of the change that has been made in the department, particularly through the introduction of a marketing branch, and some idea as to how it is being conducted and generally how the reorganization has been effected.

I think if my hon. friend will read the discussions at about this same stage last session he will find that the hon. member who is now asking the question asked it then, and an explanation was then given. I doubt very much whether I can add to it, but I am quite prepared to repeat it.
The set-up of the estimates this year indicates the intention of those of us who advocated and carried through the reorganization of the department. As I explained last year, in the estimates the items were put in the opposite way round to that which would indicate the intention of those who brought the reorganization about. This year the items appear in their natural sequence: administration service, science service, experimental farms, production service, and marketing service; and I think one has only to read those headings in order to realize that that is the natural set-up for an agriculture department. The first activity in connection with agricultural work is to make scientific investigations, not only as to what is being done in this country but as to what is being done under similar conditions in other countries, then to apply the results of that investigation on our experimental farms, and to carry that experimental work to its logical conclusion.
To illustrate, we may take the matter which was under discussion a few moments ago, that of work on rust-resistant wheat. First, certain investigations are carried out in connection with the research laboratories, not only on our farms and associated with our farm work, but also in connection with the research service generally. Then we take the results of that scientific work and apply it in the production of crops on the experimental farms. After we have produced the grain up to a certain standard and have classified it, we let

Supply-Agriculture-Administration
it out to individual farmers to multiply it. When the grain is multiplied we distribute it in two or three bushel allotments to farmers all over the western provinces, and those men by the end of one season have their own seed produced on their own farms from the distribution which is made.
That is the early stage of the work. One could apply a similar explanation in connection with the development of live stock, poultry, fruit activities, and other pursuits related to agriculture.
Then with the experience we have gained through these scientific investigations and the experimental work, we go out through the country to try to promote production. It is in the promotion of production that we have the greatest degree of assistance from the provinces. Something has been said with regard to the overlapping of our work. There is no overlapping in the scientific work. There is cooperation. We carry on activities in both scientific and experimental work in cooper

ation with the provinces, at their universities and their agricultural colleges, and we cooperate with them in the production service. The very fact that we distribute rust-resistant wheat is in itself cooperation with the provinces in the matter of production. The fact that we send overseas and purchase sires for the horse industry or the cattle industry or the sheep industry or the swine industry, assists in production generally throughout the country.
Having produced the product which we think is suited to certain markets, we try to promote the sale of that product in those markets. The larger part of the production of our farms is sold, as all hon. members know, in the Dominion of Canada. There are only three products of which we sell the greater part outside of Canada: apples, a little over 50 per cent; cheese, about 66 per cent; and wheat, about 68 per cent, the greater part being sold in Great Britain.
Our marketing activities in so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned are largely in Canada. We have a certain set-up in the old country, headed by Mr. Allen, who was sent over there last year, and who previously had been associated with the agricultural college in Saskatchewan. He heads up the service there in attempting to find out what types of live stock, for example, will best suit the market in the old country; what forms for the making up of cheese, for example, best suit that market; and determining, too, what types of fruits please that market best. This information is passed back here, and then

we utilize the different sen-ices to try to produce the kind of products which will best suit, those markets, and utilize the marketing set-up to assist in selling them.
I would say'that the difference between this set-up and the organization we had before is this. We emphasized live stock; we emphasized in another branch seeds of different kinds; we emphasized poultry in another branch; and these branches and many others were headed up by commissioners. We emphasized production and improvement in these different lines rather than what we are stressing to-day through the form of organization which is now in operation. To-day the things we emphasize are scientific investigation, experimentation, production, and marketing.

I thank the minister for his explanation of what is taking place in the department, so far as it has gone. However, these activities were largely carried on under the former organization. What I am trying to get at is this: where to go in the department when one wants certain information, or where any particular matter which one wishes to take up should be dealt with. Not so very long ago I heard a gentleman say that he came to Ottawa on some matter which had to do with poultry, and after telephoning here and there throughout the department he finally wound up in the seed branch, where he found the particular section of the department with which he wanted to deal. That is a difficulty which, as I see it, results from the lack of information which the minister has given up to the present. If you pick up the report of the minister for the last year you will find that the headings are just the same as they were previously. There is a live stock branch, a seed branch, a fruit branch, and so on down the line, with no difference or no discrimination because of the new set-up within the department.
It is just the same as it was last year.

I know it is the same. That is what we are complaining about. There should be some change. For instance, if you pick up the departmental directory you do not know to whom to appeal for any information you want within the department. Repeatedly I have called up one branch of the department and have been told, "Well, this is not the part of the department which deals with the matter at the present time." They refer me to somebody else; I speak to somebody else and find I am again in the wrong pew. That has happened repeatedly, not only to myself but to a good many other people. If

Supply-Agriculture-Administration
the minister has made these changes it is necessary that he change the directory and revise his report so that when we come to deal with these matters we shall know with whom we are to deal and where we are to go to present anything we have to present to any branch of the department. The set-up this year is exactly the same as it was when the estimates went through a year ago.

The explanation is that they have to be on the staff a certain length of time before they are permanent. He is drawing the same salary and is the same individual, but he is now on the permanent staff.

We have heard the statement made that there is overlapping between the provincial departments of agriculture and the federal department. Where is the division of responsibility, and what officers would
(Mr. Senn.]
be responsible for the liaison between the federal Department of Agriculture and the different provincial departments?

There has been a committee acting for some years to carry on discussions between the different provincial departments and this department to avoid overlapping. The last gathering for general discussion I think was about two or two and a half years ago. At that time it was decided that there was no serious overlapping between the federal and the provincial departments of agriculture, and no additions to the activities of this department have since been made which would result in further overlapping than there was then.
The provincial departments carry on in connection with agriculture in much the same way as they do in connection with other provincial activities-taking care of educational matters for example. We have no educational institutions of the type of the provincial agricultural colleges and schools. All that type of work is done by the provinces. But the general experimental work on experimental farms is done by the federal department. In the production services a greater proportion of the work is carried on by the provinces than by the dominion. In matters such as the grading of farm products there would be overlapping but for the fact that most of the provinces have appointed our inspectors as provincial inspectors in order to do much of the grading work that is done within the provinces. We have and can enforce grades for interprovincial and export trade, but we are not able to enforce those grades within the provinces themselves. In that case the provinces enact legislation setting up the same grading system as we have, and then they ask our men to become their appointees and enforce the same grading services within the province. There is no overlapping in personnel, their work is done by men who are maintained by the federal government.

Have the federal or the
local departments most to do with marketing?

do with the marketing end. All grading services come under that. We do the work, but some of the legislation is provided by the provinces.

Supply-Agriculture-Administration
the soya bean and the investigations of Doctor Carver to find new uses for the peanut. Is anything of that kind being done so far as wheat is concerned by the Department of Agriculture?

Taking the soya bean
as an example we are carrying on experiments in its breeding and production in order to suit it to different climatic conditions. But research work with regard to uses of the soya bean is carried on by the research council.

Under what department
is that?

That is under trade
and commerce, but reports are made to the Department of Agriculture.

I notice that a resolution which is on the order paper and may come before the house this session has to do with a system of dominion scholarships, a proposal which was very ably sponsored last year by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). Mention is made in the resolution of assistance in securing adequate academic training to enable young men and women to take their proper place as thoroughly trained leaders in industrial, professional and public life. Assistance is suggested for those who are unable to complete their courses in the various agricultural colleges of the dominion. In view of the large number of people who have taken a keen interest in the matter of scholarships, has the minister or his department given any consideration to the question whether or not assistance should be given by the Department of Agriculture in this connection?

As I said a while ago,
education is under provincial control; we do not directly enter that field. But we do take into the service men who have benefited from scholarships, and from time to time promising young men who, we think, would be helpful in the service in years to come we send to the universities to instruct students and to work with those who are further advanced in certain lines; then we bring them back to the department in order to make use of their services. In that sense we assist them, because we pay their salaries while they are at the universities. But we have not put up scholarships.

In connection with education I notice that at the different experimental farms throughout Canada young men are attending short courses, sometimes for four or five weeks. Forty or fifty men are attending
such a course at Fredericton. They are splendid courses and much valuable instruction is given. What arrangement is made with the local government for the payment of the expenses of these students who attend classes at the federal experimental stations?

We do not pay anything towards the expenses of the students. I understand that some provinces contribute towards the expenses of the students. But wherever we have men available we supply personnel to the provincial authorities for teaching these students, and pay them while they are doing it. And we supply our facilities at the different farms.
In Ontario are any of these instructors taking part under dominion supervision in the various short courses conducted in the different counties?

There are some, but we are not in a position to cover the whole province. They go to Kemptville and from there to other places to assist, but we cannot cover all the classes conducted in the different counties.

I believe very few educational activities, as far as young farmers are concerned, really bring about better results than the short courses conducted from time to time in the various counties of our province. Not only do they provide a type of education which is very necessary but in addition, from my experience over the last several years, they bring about a most remarkable advancement in community spirit as well. Over the years one can notice the general improvement which eventually comes to agriculture as a whole by virtue of the short courses that are given. I would suggest to the minister that any assistance he might be able to give in this work through cooperation by the federal department would be well worth while as far as the agricultural life of our dominion is concerned.

I am interested in this discussion with regard to rural education, and I have listened carefully to the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite. But for some time I have taken the view that there is great danger of overlapping our activities, and I feel that the minister would not be well advised to endeavour to go into the educational field which is so well looked after by the Ontario department of agriculture.
I was also interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) who was concerned as to where he could get certain information. That is one field in which the Ontario department has had very considerable

Supply-Agriculture-Administration
success. Anyone can go into the branch offices of the department and find racks of bulletins containing all the information that may be desired. I do not think it is the duty of the federal department to establish an information bureau especially for the members of parliament; that is not particularly our business. When we go home for week-ends we can go to the branch office and get any information we want.
I believe we spend a great deal of money unnecessarily because of the overlapping of these services. I sometimes question the advisability of maintaining a central experimental farm here in Ottawa when we have such splendid farms in each province. I sometimes wonder if that money could not be spent better in other directions. I do not claim to be an authority on the subject, but this is one of the things that come into the mind of the average farmer to make him wonder whether we are getting the best possible value for the money we spend. The government is asked to do so many things. A question was raised this evening in connection with supplying seed wheat, and as an Ontario farmer I marvel at the ability of our western men-whom I always look upon as masters of brilliant intellect-to be spoon-fed, as I think the hon. member for Parkdale put it a couple of years ago. No doubt that was how he came to coin the phrase. They expect the government to supply them with seed wheat. Down in Ontario we try to make our own effort, and I think the minister is to be commended on attempting to bring out a little self-reliance in some of these people, even though they may have to drive twenty-five miles. If they cannot afford to buy rust-resistant wheat why not do as I have to do when I want some new variety? I buy a bushel or two and sow it, and then I have my seed for next year. I have no money to spend extravagantly. If I want a team of horses I generally sell the S200 horse and buy $50 colts, and I think if the farmers in the west would do something like that they would not have so many difficulties.
I want to come back to the question of education. I hope the minister will not be induced, by the very able speech of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), to duplicate the educational activities which are so well administered by the province. I am quite a believer in the school of experience. So far as scholarships are concerned, I am doubtful whether any service could be rendered in that way. Not long ago my attention was drawn to the type of men who are at the head of the United States Steel Corporation and the Standard Oil Company. Of course this is a little

outside agriculture, but they are two of the largest concerns on the north American continent. I noticed that the men at the head of those two firms were poor boys, raised on farms and having the benefit of only a very limited public school education. That would seem to prove that there is something in the atmosphere of the farm which, if properly applied, brings out the ability that is in a man. True, he must be able to develop his mental capacity, but I am not so sure that we derive any substantial results from some of these scholarships, which by the way are very expensive; I am not sure that those who have benefited have really made any important contribution to the nation as a result of these expenditures.
These are just some thoughts I have picked up from my association with men living in my own atmosphere, but I think they are worth considering. Let me say once more that I hope the minister will not be lured, by the fine speeches of those opposite, into broadening out into a wider sphere when I think perhaps we have too much duplication already.
I would suggest that if any of the friends of my hon. friend try to get a position in the civil service in connection with agriculture he will see how far they get without a scholarship.

I always sympathize with anyone who applies to the civil service commission or the government for a position. It is one of the last places I would want to work, and really I do not advise any of my friends to apply for government jobs.

I should like to take this
opportunity of thanking my colleague and neighbour the member for Brant (Mr. Wood) for telling me just where I can get all the information that may be required in connection with agriculture throughout the dominion. I had thought, of course, that certain information could be better obtained from the federal department than could be found in the archives or publications of any particular province.
I have been surprised at the scope of this discussion, having in mind what the minister said a few moments ago when I was trying to get him to lay certain papers on the table. He said that request was rather wide of the mark in discussion of this particular item, but since then we have gone considerably further afield. The minister chose to ignore what I thought was a very reasonable request, that this information should be tabled, but I am going to make another appeal to him. After all, this gentleman is

Supply-National Revenue-Customs
a paid official of the government; public money is expended in paying his salary and expenses, and I think the information he sends back to the Department of Agriculture should be made available to parliament. If there is anything that is confidential, that is a different matter, but I do not see why there should be anything confidential in a public servant,giving information to his minister or to the department which he is serving. I make one more appeal to the minister to allow that correspondence and information to be placed on the table for the use of members of this house, because I think it will assist him in getting his estimates through.

I hope the hon. member did not think I was ignoring the matter.
I simply stated that it was departmental correspondence. I do not know that it would be of any particular use to the house in its present form. I have no objection to its being brought down, which might be done through an order for return; or I can bring it down and lay it on the table when we discuss the matter again. However, I do think it would be very much more useful if, before bringing it down, we put the information in some sort of shape that would make it more easily understood. I do not think anyone would want to go through a file of departmental letters written back and forth, but if they are wanted I can bring them down.

I have no desire to embarrass the minister or to find out anything that is at all confidential. On the other hand the very remarks which might be most important might be left out of any report that was made. What the minister might consider unimportant other members of the committee might regard as important. I am making what I think is a reasonable request when I ask that the information be tabled.
Item agreed to.

Customs and excise divisions-
218. General administration, $972,135.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I desire only that the item be called; there is really no time for any discussion on it to-night. I would ask that it stand.

Mr. Chairman, I would refer hon. members to a statement made last night at the adjournment hour, when the Prime Minister was asked about the business for to-day. The right hon. gentleman said:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	To-morrow we shall
take up the resolution with respect to the trade agreement between Canada and the United States. I understand there is a desire not to proceed with the debate to-morrow in which event we would go on with supply, and take the estimates for the Department of Agriculture, Public Works or National Revenue.
That is open to the interpretation of taking only one department. I have no objection to taking two, but I do not think we ought to go into more than two.
Did he say " or " or " and"?
"Or."
" Or " means " and."
It does not mean " and," in that connection.
Did the Prime Minister say " the Department of National Revenue, the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Public Works "?
He said ".... take the estimates for the Department of Agriculture, Public Works or National Revenue." That means one department, if it means anything.
Two.
We have admitted two.
What is the matter with three?
I think two is enough.
We can easily stop it by discussing the item which has just been called.
We ought to go into two departments, according to the understanding, and no more. That is enough to keep us going.
Is there a desire on the part of the acting leader of the opposition to take four departments to-night?

I do not think that question requires an answer at all. If the hon. member was listening he would know I said that the Prime Minister's statement meant one department. Why should I say four departments?

It seems so foolish, when the department is available and when members are willing, that the hon. member who is acting as leader of the opposition should try to delay those departments getting into supply.

The minister can go back to item 218.
{The Chairman.]
We can discuss item 218, then, if hon. members wish.
Carried.

Will the minister be good enough to make an explanation of this item? There seems to be some change in the classification of appraisers-either that, or there is a large increase in salaries. About one-third of the way down on page 138 there are items of S4,000, $16,000 and $19,000, in round figures, in the estimates for 1939-40. Then there is an item of $10,260 in the estimates for 193839, which does not appear in the figures for the ensuing year. Do those relate to the same subject matter?

Yes; there has been a reclassification, which means that there are fewer customs reviewing appraisers, and therefore a decrease under that item. There are more dominion customs appraisers, and therefore an increase under those items. Unless there is some offsetting decrease elsewhere, which at the moment I do not see, there has been apparently a net increase.
Apparently the increase is in the neighbourhood of $30,000. That seems extraordinary in one year, by a mere reclassification, unless there are a great many more appraisers.
The number is increased, as indicated in the first column on the page under the figures 1939-40.
Apparently there is an increase up to thirteen or fourteen, whereas previously there were only three. What is the reason for the increase?

There have been some
transfers from other classifications. For instance, lower down on the page there is a decrease of seventeen customs reviewing appraisers, grade 1. That is about three-quarters of the way down the page.
But right above that there is an increase of eight, again.
There the balance is the other way.
And an increase of sixteen in the next item below that.

One would have to go
through all the items to see whether or not there had been a net increase.

Has not the minister available a memorandum showing the reason for these changes in classification, what the result has been, and how much more money it is costing the taxpayers?

Supply-National Revenue-Customs
It is not costing us more.
There has been an increase in salaries for the appraisers branch. The authorized compensation for 1938-39 was $151,965.
That is for appraisers only?
That is in the appraisers' branch. The estimated compensation for 1939-40 is $172,535. Part of that is accounted for by statutory increases which amount to $5,370.
That would leave about $15,000 for new employees?
That is it.
How many new appraisers have been created-on balance, I mean?
The $15,000 would not be entirely for new employees. There are increases in salaries.
I deducted the statutory increases.
There are increases that are not statutory, due to reclassification of positions.
Could the minister tell me, on balance, how many more appraisers it is proposed to have for 1939-10?
If the hon. gentleman wants that exactly-
Approximately.
Approximately there is no change.
There may have been one or two appointments, but nothing beyond that?
That sums up the situation.
I understand appraisers are not appointed by the civil service commission.
Yes, they are.
Do they not come under the national revenue act?
They do. but I do not exercise my powers under that act. The civil service commission appoints them all.
Has there been any general reduction in staff throughout the whole department?

This item may be a little misleading. There has been a transfer of quite a number of officers from national
revenue to trade and commerce. The statistical branch has been moved from national revenue to trade and commerce.

I think the minister is to be complimented upon not using his powers under the national revenue act. There is another matter I should like to discuss under this item. I should like to know who is responsible for the issuance of regulations in connection with appraisals, and so on, particularly in connection with the hundred dollar tourist exemption. Last year I drew the attention of the minister to the regulations that had been issued. For example, if automobile tires were on the wheels of a car they were dutiable, and if clothing was being worn it was dutiable. At that time the minister made a statement and I believe he read the regulation. As I recall it, the regulation is that an article can be brought in under this exemption if contained within baggage. I am sorry I did not bring the particular Hansard down with me, but as I remember it the resolution of parliament was that this exemption should include articles included in baggage. There is a distinct difference between "contained within" and "included in." An article might be shipped by rail and be included in, but not contained within, baggage. It seems to me that what has occurred in connection with this particular item is a gradual increase in the restrictions which has to a large extent eliminated the intention of parliament.
No.

The minister says "no," but I put this before him so that he can clear it up. I note that the balance as between Canada and the United States is greatly in favour of Canada. American tourists buy much more in Canada than Canadian tourists buy in the United States.
I do not know, because there are no statistics to show.
There are estimates.
I have never seen any estimates of what the Americans buy here under the hundred dollar exemption.

I have seen them from time to time. I think it is quite logical one should make such an estimate, because more Americans enter Canada to buy woollen goods, chinaware and other things. When Canadians from western Canada cross the border into the United States, very often they have no money with which to purchase goods in that country.

There is a greater variety of goods purchased in the United States.
Trade Agreements-Policy

I just wanted to bring this to the attention of the minister. I notice that the United States regulations have been tightened up to meet ours. Not long ago an American tourist could enter this country, remain a few hours to purchase goods, and then go back. To-day he must remain forty-eight hours, the same as Canadians have to remain in the United States.
We did not tighten up ours.

I am pointing out these things because I believe the intention of parliament was one thing and the regulations are another. I notice it is close to eleven o'clock, and I shall discuss this matter at another time. In spite of the fact that we talk about lowering the barriers against goods coming into this country, the method of appraising for duty purposes retains at all times about the same amount of protection as when we had a relatively higher tariff. I think that that is correct in many instances, although not in all.
Progress reported.
